questions.stem: In 1517 Martin Luther wrote his Ninety-five Theses mainly to criticise:
options: the printing of the Bible in German
the sale of indulgences by the Church
the growing power of the Ottoman sultan
the marriages of King Henry VIII
questions.explanation: Luther objected to preachers such as Johann Tetzel selling indulgences, which promised to reduce punishment for sins in exchange for money. Luther later translated the Bible into German himself, so he was certainly not against German Bibles.

questions.stem: What was an indulgence in the Catholic Church of Luther's time?
options: A licence that allowed a merchant to trade on Sundays
A written promise of protection and land given by a feudal lord to a vassal
A reduction of punishment for sins after death, granted by the Church
A tax paid to the king for the right to hold land from him
questions.explanation: The Church taught that an indulgence could reduce the time a soul spent being punished in purgatory, and by the early 1500s they were being sold to raise money, including for rebuilding St Peter's in Rome. Luther argued that forgiveness came from God and could not be bought.

questions.stem: Why did Luther's ideas spread so quickly across Germany?
options: The Holy Roman Emperor ordered every school to teach Luther's ideas
Printing presses turned out thousands of cheap copies of his writings
The pope sent copies of Luther's writings to every parish church in Europe
Luther travelled to every German town to preach his ideas in person
questions.explanation: Printing had reached Germany about seventy years earlier, and Luther's short pamphlets in German were printed and sold in huge numbers. The emperor Charles V actually condemned Luther as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms in 1521.

questions.stem: Which was a key belief of Luther and the other Protestant reformers?
options: Salvation comes through faith, and the Bible is the final authority
The pope's teachings rank above the Bible as the final authority
Salvation comes mainly through buying indulgences and relics
Only priests should read the Bible, and only ever in Latin
questions.explanation: Protestants taught that people are saved by faith in God's grace, and that the Bible, not the pope or Church tradition, is the final authority. They wanted ordinary people to read the Bible in their own language, the opposite of keeping it in Latin for priests.

questions.stem: John Calvin led the Reformation from which city, where he helped set up a strict Protestant government?
options: Geneva
Rome
Seville
Vienna
questions.explanation: Calvin made Geneva, in present-day Switzerland, a centre of Protestant teaching from the 1540s, and his ideas spread to Scotland, the Netherlands and France. Rome was the centre of the Catholic Church.

questions.stem: What was the Counter-Reformation?
options: The Catholic Church's own reforms in response to Protestantism
A Protestant movement to rejoin the Catholic Church
England's break with Rome under King Henry VIII
A treaty that ended the wars of religion by banning Protestantism everywhere
questions.explanation: The Catholic Church answered Protestantism by reforming itself — the Council of Trent (1545–1563) tackled abuses and restated Catholic beliefs — and new orders such as the Jesuits spread Catholic education. It strengthened Catholicism rather than seeking to join Protestant churches.

questions.stem: The Act of Supremacy of 1534 made whom the Supreme Head of the Church of England?
options: Pope Clement VII
Martin Luther
Elizabeth I
King Henry VIII
questions.explanation: Parliament's Act of Supremacy declared Henry VIII head of the English Church in place of the pope. Elizabeth I became Supreme Governor of the Church under a later Act of 1559, after her Catholic sister Mary had restored papal authority.

questions.stem: Why did Henry VIII break with the Church in Rome?
options: The pope ordered him to hand the English throne to the King of Spain
He had become a follower of Luther and rejected the Catholic Mass
Parliament forced him to adopt John Calvin's teachings
The pope refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon
questions.explanation: Henry wanted a male heir and sought to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon so he could marry Anne Boleyn; when the pope would not agree, Henry made himself head of the English Church. He kept many Catholic beliefs and had earlier written against Luther, earning the title 'Defender of the Faith'.

questions.stem: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus published the idea that:
options: the Earth and the other planets travel around the Sun
the Sun and the other planets travel around the Earth
the Earth sits still while the stars travel around the Sun
the planets travel around the Moon, which circles the Earth
questions.explanation: Copernicus proposed a heliocentric (Sun-centred) model, challenging the ancient geocentric model of Ptolemy in which everything circled the Earth. The Earth-centred view was the one the Church and most scholars had accepted for centuries.

questions.stem: What did Johannes Kepler discover about the paths of the planets?
options: They travel around the Sun in elliptical paths
They travel around the Sun in perfect circles
They travel around the Earth in elliptical paths
They stand still while the Sun moves among them
questions.explanation: Kepler showed in the early 1600s that planetary orbits are ellipses (stretched circles), which made the Sun-centred model match observations far better. Copernicus had kept the ancient idea of perfect circles, which is why his model did not fit the data well.

questions.stem: Why was Galileo put on trial by the Roman Inquisition in 1633?
options: He refused to look through his telescope at the night sky
He translated the Bible into Italian without permission
He defended the view that the Earth moves around the Sun
He claimed the Earth was flat and that the Church was wrong
questions.explanation: Galileo's telescope observations, such as moons orbiting Jupiter, supported Copernicus, and his 1632 book defended a moving Earth; the Inquisition forced him to recant and kept him under house arrest. Educated Europeans had known the Earth was round since ancient times, so flatness was never the issue.

questions.stem: What did Isaac Newton show in his Principia, published in 1687?
options: The heavens follow different laws of motion from objects on Earth
The Sun travels around the Earth, pulled along by its gravity
One law of gravity explains falling apples and orbiting planets
Heavier objects always fall faster than lighter ones in all cases
questions.explanation: Newton's law of universal gravitation showed that the same force pulls an apple to the ground and keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits. This overturned the old idea, from Aristotle, that the heavens obeyed completely different rules from the Earth.

questions.stem: Why did the Scientific Revolution challenge the authority of the Church?
options: Its scientists were all atheists who wanted to close down every church in Europe
It proved that the Bible contained no true statements at all
It was led by kings who wanted to seize the Church's lands
It said claims should be tested by observation, not accepted on authority
questions.explanation: Thinkers such as Galileo and Francis Bacon argued that knowledge should come from observation, measurement and experiment, so long-accepted teachings could be tested and overturned. Many scientists, including Kepler and Newton, were deeply religious; the challenge was to the source of authority, not to faith itself.

questions.stem: What did the Enlightenment thinker John Locke argue about government?
options: All property should be shared, with no private wealth at all
People have natural rights, and government rests on their consent
Kings rule by divine right and must never be questioned
People are naturally wicked and need an all-powerful ruler
questions.explanation: Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a government which breaks its trust can rightly be replaced; these ideas influenced the American Declaration of Independence. The view that people need an all-powerful ruler to control them belongs to Thomas Hobbes, not Locke.

questions.stem: The French thinker Montesquieu argued that, to protect liberty:
options: power should be divided among legislative, executive and judicial branches
all power should be held by one monarch chosen and guided by God
the Church should appoint the judges and run all of the law courts
citizens should vote directly on every single law, with no parliament at all
questions.explanation: In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that separating law-making, carrying out the law and judging cases stops any one person or group becoming a tyrant. Australia's Constitution follows this idea in separating the parliament, the executive and the courts.

questions.stem: King Louis XIV of France, who built the palace of Versailles, is a classic example of:
options: an absolute monarch
a constitutional monarch
an elected president
a Protestant reformer
questions.explanation: Louis XIV ruled from 1643 to 1715 without calling France's representative assembly, the Estates-General, and claimed his power came from God. A constitutional monarch, by contrast, rules within limits set by law and a parliament.

questions.stem: What happened to King Charles I of England in 1649?
options: He was executed after losing the Civil War to Parliament
He was crowned king after defeating Oliver Cromwell
He was made Supreme Head of the Church by the pope
He fled to France during the Glorious Revolution
questions.explanation: After Parliament's armies defeated him in the English Civil War, Charles I was tried for treason and beheaded in January 1649. The Glorious Revolution of 1688 removed a different king, his son James II.

questions.stem: After the execution of Charles I, Oliver Cromwell ruled England with which title?
options: Archbishop of Canterbury
Lord Protector
King of England
Prime Minister
questions.explanation: Cromwell refused the crown and ruled as Lord Protector from 1653 until his death in 1658; the monarchy was restored under Charles II in 1660. The office of Prime Minister did not develop until the 1700s.

questions.stem: Why is the English Civil War seen as a step towards the Westminster system that Australia uses?
options: It made the pope the final judge of disputes between king and Parliament
It began to establish that a monarch must govern with Parliament's consent
It made England a permanent republic with no king or queen ever again
It gave every adult man and woman in England the right to vote
questions.explanation: The war and the later Glorious Revolution of 1688 settled that the monarch could not rule, tax or keep an army without Parliament, the basis of today's parliamentary system. England was a republic only from 1649 to 1660, and votes for all adults came centuries later.

questions.stem: In France before 1789, society was divided into three estates. Who belonged to the Third Estate?
options: The nobles, who owned much of the land and paid little tax
The clergy, from village priests up to bishops and abbots
The king, the royal family and the courtiers and servants who lived at Versailles
Everyone outside the clergy and nobility, from peasants to merchants
questions.explanation: Under the Ancien Régime the clergy formed the First Estate and the nobility the Second; the Third Estate was everyone else — around 97 per cent of the people — and it carried most of the tax burden. Resentment of this system helped cause the French Revolution.
